channel_name: No Priors · Elad Gil & Sarah Guo
video_title: Re-Founding Incumbents for the AI Era with Sequence Holdings Co-Founder and CEO Michael Lee
gist: Michael Lee (ex-Lone Pine, Apollo, Goldman) explains Sequence Holdings, a perpetual holding company that buys stakes in incumbent market leaders and re-engineers them around AI with an in-house frontier engineering team. He covers the $7.7B take-private of insurance broker Baldwin with the Dell family office, and early results at community bank BankSouth: consumer-loan underwriting down 94%, commercial loans cut from 30 to 11 days, and loan volume doubling with no added staff. Note: the auto-caption transcript reads like a machine translation, so some wording and figures are garbled.

themes.theme: Why incumbents plus ownership win the AI transition

insights.claim: Michael Lee's core thesis is that AI will affect the economy unevenly. Some sectors, like restaurants and golf courses, will barely change. In some, like coding, startups such as Cognition or Anthropic will win. In many others, incumbent leaders keep their brand, scale, network-effect and regulatory advantages and can become the AI-era leaders if they are re-engineered.
insights.speaker: Michael Lee (Sequence Holdings CEO)
insights.so_what: Sort sectors into three groups (untouched, startup-disrupted, incumbent-advantaged) to decide whether to back AI-native startups or AI-transformed incumbents.

insights.claim: Lee argues that most enterprise AI deployments give each worker on today's 'human assembly line' a small helper, which he calls better than nothing. The bigger value comes from redesigning the whole organization around machines that run 24/7 and scale with electricity.
insights.speaker: Michael Lee (Sequence Holdings CEO)
insights.so_what: Copilot-style seat tools may capture less value than owners who redesign workflows end to end, which is a caution for per-seat AI software valuations.

insights.claim: Lee sees three options for an incumbent CEO, each with a structural flaw. Building in-house fails because the company cannot attract or keep elite engineers when its celebrated figure is not the engineer. Consultancies and service firms such as Accenture, McKinsey and Palantir are paid to grow their share of the client's wallet, which leads to incremental change. Bought software is available to every competitor and hard-codes today's workflow.
insights.speaker: Michael Lee (Sequence Holdings CEO)
insights.so_what: Suggests a ceiling on how deeply IT services and vertical SaaS can transform incumbents, and supports ownership-based AI roll-up models.
insights.quote: Service companies optimize their costs for three things: getting funds into your wallet, keeping them in your wallet, and increasing your wallet share. This is the path to gradualism.

insights.claim: Lee says vertical software vendors have to sell workflows as they exist today, because a product built for a reorganized, AI-native workflow that doesn't exist yet has no buyers. Owners can redesign the org chart, roles and incentives themselves.
insights.speaker: Michael Lee (Sequence Holdings CEO)
insights.so_what: Vertical SaaS incumbents may be poorly placed to capture AI-driven organizational redesign, while operators who own the business capture it instead.

insights.claim: Lee calls Palantir essentially a wrapper that gathers and celebrates world-class engineers and sells that talent to organizations that can't recruit it. Engineer-centric culture is the scarce asset in AI transformation.
insights.speaker: Michael Lee (Sequence Holdings CEO)
insights.so_what: Supports the value of engineer-led platforms such as Palantir and explains why investor-led firms struggle to build this capability in-house.
insights.quote: In a world where you believe alpha comes from engineering and artificial intelligence, you need to create a culture where the persona of note is the engineer.

themes.theme: Sequence's perpetual holdco vs private equity

insights.claim: Sequence Holdings is set up as a perpetual holding company rather than a fund. The goal is to match long-duration capital to multi-year transformation work, build one shared engineering platform across portfolio companies, and reinvest retained earnings, with no fund-style pressure to deploy or exit.
insights.speaker: Michael Lee (Sequence Holdings CEO)
insights.so_what: Permanent-capital AI holdcos are a new competitor to traditional buyout funds for incumbent assets, especially in sectors where the payoff takes a long time.

insights.claim: Lee lists three limits on how far traditional buyout firms can transform companies with AI. Their culture celebrates investors, so a 25-year-old engineer rarely has a say in deals. Fund timelines push toward packaging an asset for sale within about 3 years. Deployment cadence pushes them to invest. He still expects many PE firms to make significant progress.
insights.speaker: Michael Lee (Sequence Holdings CEO)
insights.so_what: Suggests that value from AI transformation in PE-owned companies may fall short of the pitch, and that permanent-capital owners could outbid funds for AI-transformable assets.
insights.quote: You're usually trying to figure out how we're going to start preparing packages to sell this thing in 3 years .

insights.claim: Sequence aims to do about one deal a year, has no deployment cadence and no investors pushing it to invest, and Lee says he hopes to hold Sequence's positions for the rest of his life.
insights.speaker: Michael Lee (Sequence Holdings CEO)
insights.so_what: Deal flow will be sparse and concentrated, so each announced Sequence deal signals which sectors it thinks incumbents will win in AI.
insights.quote: We try to do one deal a year. That's all.

insights.claim: Lee says Sequence's model is independent of AI model progress: each improvement in frontier models (Anthropic, OpenAI, xAI) gives it more tools, whereas application-layer software startups face existential risk from better models. He uses this in recruiting engineers.
insights.speaker: Michael Lee (Sequence Holdings CEO)
insights.so_what: AI-transformed owners of real businesses are hedged against model commoditization, unlike thin application-layer wrappers.

themes.theme: Baldwin $7.7B take-private with Dell family office

insights.claim: Sequence Holdings and the Dell family office agreed to acquire insurance broker Baldwin for $7.7 billion. The show calls it the largest private AI-driven acquisition to date. The two will co-manage Baldwin, and Lee credits Michael Dell and the office's head of global private equity with underwriting both the deal and Sequence's technology platform.
insights.speaker: host / Michael Lee
insights.so_what: Large family offices are now backing multi-billion-dollar AI-transformation take-privates, a model that could reprice publicly listed insurance brokers and similar incumbents.

insights.claim: Lee says insurance brokerage is a strong target for AI-driven incumbents. More than $2 trillion a year in premiums flows through the market, it has produced dozens of large, skilled companies, client retention is about 90%, and startups struggle to break in because the insurer pays the broker, brokers can't compete on price, and the business runs on relationships.
insights.speaker: Michael Lee (Sequence Holdings CEO)
insights.so_what: Insurance brokers look shielded from startup disruption while still able to capture AI efficiency gains, which is constructive for scaled brokers that modernize.

insights.claim: Lee argues that insurers have made almost no money from underwriting historically and earn most of their profit from investing float. That pushes them to accumulate assets and to value quality premium growth, which makes the distribution (broker) layer powerful.
insights.speaker: Michael Lee (Sequence Holdings CEO)
insights.so_what: Explains why brokers keep pricing power with carriers, which supports durable broker economics.
insights.quote: The insurance industry has made almost no money from underwriting since the beginning of time.

insights.claim: Sequence chose Baldwin partly because it was already technology-forward. CEO Trevor Baldwin had rolled out Anthropic across the company, and it runs on a single instance of Applied Epic, the agency management system Lee describes as the insurance broker's core operating system.
insights.speaker: Michael Lee (Sequence Holdings CEO)
insights.so_what: Consolidated data systems and existing frontier-model adoption are becoming screening criteria for AI-transformation buyers, which gives companies that have done that groundwork a premium.

insights.claim: Sequence's first investment grew out of a service engagement from August to November with a Georgia bank owned by the family of Avenir co-founder Jamie Reynolds. It became a permanent minority stake that closed in March after Fed and OCC approval, which solved Sequence's cold-start problem.
insights.speaker: Michael Lee (Sequence Holdings CEO)
insights.so_what: Shows how AI holdcos can move from service engagement to equity stake. Bank deals carry regulatory approval delays of several months.

insights.claim: About six months after investing, Sequence says BankSouth's consumer-loan underwriting (the transcript calls it 'volume', probably meaning time or effort) is down 94%, and commercial-loan turnaround is down from about 30 days to 11 days.
insights.speaker: Michael Lee (Sequence Holdings CEO)
insights.so_what: Concrete productivity numbers from AI agents in regulated lending, and a benchmark for what community and regional banks could achieve on middle- and back-office costs.
insights.quote: which used to take 30 days, down to 11 days

insights.claim: BankSouth's loan volume in Q2 doubled from Q1, and Lee says the bank handled it without changing underwriting standards and with fewer underwriters: one retired and one moved to the front office. Before, the bank had turned away customers because loan volume grew linearly with middle- and back-office headcount.
insights.speaker: Michael Lee (Sequence Holdings CEO)
insights.so_what: AI can separate bank loan growth from operations headcount, which would improve efficiency ratios and operating leverage for early-adopting banks.

insights.claim: Lee argues that a bank's regulated nature helps AI deployment: defined operating rules and good data hygiene suit agents. Centralized underwriting means anything built at headquarters is amortized across every branch.
insights.speaker: Michael Lee (Sequence Holdings CEO)
insights.so_what: Heavily regulated, centralized industries such as banking and insurance may be early AI winners rather than laggards, against the usual view that regulation slows adoption.
insights.quote: the regulated nature of the bank was a feature, not a mistake

themes.theme: Target selection and the Atlas platform

insights.claim: Sequence screens targets on 'organizational physics'. It prefers dense, centralized organizations over sprawling multi-site roll-ups, which need system integration, engineers on site and standardized procedures. It also wants a large market, incumbent-favoring industry structure, and a good overlap between what the company does and what AI does well today.
insights.speaker: Michael Lee (Sequence Holdings CEO)
insights.so_what: A usable screen for which incumbents can most cheaply capture AI operating leverage: centralized operations and a single system of record.

insights.claim: Sequence's Atlas platform was built at the bank and is meant to generalize across industries. It has four layers: a data ontology that describes the business in code, an agent builder, an orchestration layer called 'lattice', and an application builder called 'artifacts'. It rests on the observation that about 80% of a business's atomic units are homogeneous and about 20% are vertical-specific.
insights.speaker: Michael Lee (Sequence Holdings CEO)
insights.so_what: A reusable cross-industry platform is the lever that could let AI holdcos earn more on each additional acquisition, so watch for evidence that the Baldwin rollout reuses the BankSouth infrastructure.
insights.quote: if you break down a business into its atomic units, 80% of them are largely homogeneous and 20% are vertically specific

insights.claim: Lee says the human side of transformation (employee anxiety, change management, keeping people engaged) is much harder than the engineering. Sequence therefore partners with existing management teams that already know their industry and have started modernizing: moved to the cloud, centralized data, deployed OpenAI or Anthropic.
insights.speaker: Michael Lee (Sequence Holdings CEO)
insights.so_what: Execution risk in AI roll-ups is mainly organizational, so judge AI-transformation stories by management quality and change management, not just the tech stack.

themes.theme: Investing lessons from Lone Pine to Sequence

insights.claim: Lee, who covered AI at Lone Pine from 2017, says ChatGPT's arrival in late 2022 showed that the world had changed forever. For the first time there was an architecture that could keep improving with more compute, unlike earlier CNN, GAN and LSTM approaches that ran into limits as they scaled.
insights.speaker: Michael Lee (Sequence Holdings CEO)
insights.so_what: A former public-markets investor views scaling laws as the core long-term driver behind AI economic impact.

insights.claim: Lee says betting on exceptional people working on hard problems in big markets is what matters most in both venture and public markets. He cites meeting Nvidia's Jensen Huang in 2017 as the best example. From Lone Pine he learned that the best companies, such as Nvidia, Microsoft and Visa, compound at rates few expect.
insights.speaker: Michael Lee (Sequence Holdings CEO)
insights.so_what: Supports underwriting founders and CEOs first, and holding top compounders for the long run.
